<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README contents, this project is a JavaScript charting library (ApexCharts) designed to allow users to easily create and integrate interactive, configurable charts into their applications. The project is structured as a library (rather than a full-stack web app) and includes a well-organized source (src) with modules for different chart types and supporting functionalities, a build system to compile the source code into distributable formats (in the dist folder), a rich set of samples (demonstrating usage with various frameworks like React, Vue, and vanilla JS), and extensive tests.

Below are detailed guidelines to create a system design (architecture) diagram tailored to this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Core Library: The main entry point is in src/apexcharts.js which orchestrates the initialization and rendering of charts.
   • Chart Type Implementations: Located in src/charts, this folder contains individual files for different charts (e.g., Bar.js, Line.js, Treemap.js). Each file encapsulates the logic for drawing that specific chart type.
   • Modules (Features & Functionalities): Under src/modules you find specialized functionalities such as annotations, axes, tooltips, legends, settings, and utilities. These modules provide discrete features (like formatting, interactivity, crosshair, and zoom/pan) and are used in assembling the charts.
   • Assets & Localizations:
         - Assets (src/assets): Contains required stylesheets (CSS) for the library.
         - Locales (src/locales): Includes JSON files for internationalization support.
   • Libraries & Utilities:
         - src/libs holds additional helper libraries (e.g., for Treemap calculations or monotone cubic curves).
         - src/utils provides common helper functions like DateTime utilities and responsive Resize handling.
   • Build & Distribution:
         - The build folder (with scripts like build.js/config.js) and configuration files (e.g., webpack.config.js, babel.config.js) govern the build process.
         - Final distributable files are located in the dist folder in various module formats (AMD, CommonJS, ESM).
   • Samples & Tests:
         - The samples directory contains demo code for usage in various frameworks (React, Vue, vanilla JS, etc.), showing integration patterns.
         - The tests folder (with both unit and end-to-end tests) validates functionality and ensures code quality.
   • External Dependency:
         - The project uses SVG.js for the actual DOM/SVG drawing. Although bundled in the build, this dependency forms a critical layer for rendering graphics.

2. Map Relationships and Interactions:
   • The API (exposed via the core entry file) accepts user configuration (chart options) and routes the requests to the appropriate chart type module.
   • Each chart type module then uses multiple modules for added functionality (for example, tooltips, axes rendering, annotations) to build the visualizations.
   • The modules communicate with utility functions to handle common concerns like responsive resizing, date-time formatting, and SVG manipulation (via SVG.js).
   • The build system collects these components, transforms them (using Babel/webpack), and outputs the final distributable libraries in the dist folder.
   • The samples illustrate integration with various frameworks, highlighting the library’s flexibility as an embeddable charting tool.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modular design: The project is very modular, separating chart types, UI functionalities, and support utilities into identifiably distinct folders.
   • Separation of concerns: Each module (e.g., axes, tooltip, legend, annotations) encapsulates a specific functionality and can be updated independently.
   • Reusability: Common helper functions and utility modules reduce code duplication and provide reusable functionality across multiple chart types.
   • Extensibility: Since each chart type is implemented in its own file, new charts or features can be added without impacting existing code.
   • Build orchestration: The use of a clear build pipeline (via webpack, Babel) indicates a well-structured modernization process for code transformation and distribution.

4. Tailoring the Diagram:
   • Represent layers in your diagram:
         - At the top, the “API / Core Engine” for chart initialization.
         - The “Chart Types Layer” (listing Bar, Line, Pie, etc.).
         - The “Modules Layer” which includes sub-modules (axes, annotations, tooltips, legends, settings, events, responsive behavior).
         - The “Utilities & Libraries Layer” (helpers and external libraries such as SVG.js).
         - The “Build & Distribution” layer, showing the transformation from src through build scripts to the final dist folder.
         - Additionally, you might note supporting components like “Samples” and “Tests” as auxiliary elements that facilitate integration and quality assurance.
   • Use directional arrows to show the flow:
         - From user code → Core API, then to Chart Modules → Sub-modules → Utility functions → Rendering (via SVG.js).
         - Also show that build scripts transform the source structure into the final distributable outputs.
   • Use color-coding or different shapes:
         - E.g., use different colors for “Business Logic” (chart types and modules), “Support Utilities” (libs, utils), and “Infrastructure” (build scripts and configuration).
         - Clearly label external dependencies (for instance, a box around SVG.js to denote its role in rendering).

5. Diagram Elements to Include:
   • Clear labels for each component, for example:
         - “Core Engine (src/apexcharts.js)”
         - “Chart Modules (src/charts/*)” – list a few exemplars like Bar, Line, Pie.
         - “Feature Modules (src/modules/)” – group by functionalities (e.g., axes, annotations, tooltips).
         - “Assets & Locales (src/assets, src/locales)”
         - “Utilities (src/utils, src/libs)”
         - “Build Process (build/, webpack.config.js, babel.config.js)”
         - “Distribution (dist/)”
         - “Samples & Tests (samples/, tests/)”
   • Directional arrows to indicate data flow and dependencies:
         - From the core entry point to the various modules.
         - From modules to utility functions and to the external dependency (SVG.js).
   • Color coding or different shapes to help visually separate:
         - Core components, support modules, and external systems.
         - Optionally include wrappers (React/Vue/Angular integration) as additional adapter layers positioned externally.

6. Final Thoughts for the Diagram:
   • Keep the diagram detailed – do not simply create a high-level box labeled “apexcharts.” Instead, break it down into as many relevant functional blocks as possible.
   • Use arrows to detail how the various modules communicate (for example, the core engine calls chart type logic, which in turn calls tooltip or axes modules).
   • Make sure to highlight the build process which converts the source structure in “src” into usable artifacts in “dist.”
   • Ensure clear labeling to help any viewer (especially other engineers or architects) quickly grasp how the charting engine fabricates interactive visualizations using modular components.

Following these instructions, you will create a comprehensive system design diagram that accurately reflects the architecture of the ApexCharts project, showcasing its modular design, clear separation of responsibilities, and the full journey from configuration and API consumption to rendering graphical charts with SVG.js.
</explanation>
